opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I find this genuinely mysterious, and I don't think I have a satisfying answer.

Here's what puzzles me. Some desires are easy to explain. If you want evolution to make you like the smell of good food, that's straightforward: there's a chemical, there's a receptor, and you wire the receptor to the reward signal. Simple, low-level, close to the sensors. You can imagine a genome encoding that.

But we also care about extremely abstract things. We care about social standing, about whether people think well of us, about being seen as fair, about our reputation within a group. Those aren't smells. To even know whether you're being respected, your brain has to do a lot of processing: model other people, interpret their tone, infer their intentions. The "thing" you care about only exists at the end of a long computation, somewhere high up in the cortex. And yet evolution somehow made us care about it, and pretty reliably across people.

So how does the genome point at that? The genome doesn't know where in the brain a particular concept will end up. It's not like there's a fixed neuron for "my tribe respects me." Learning shapes all of that.

You could speculate. Maybe evolution said, roughly, "a certain brain region, which tends to end up representing social information because of its connectivity, is wired to the reward system." That kind of story works if the location is stable. But brains are quite plastic, and people with significant damage early on still develop rich social drives, so that explanation feels incomplete to me.

Maybe it's bootstrapped: start with simple innate signals, like faces, smiles, a mother's voice, and learning attaches more and more abstract things to them over time. That's probably part of it.

But the real reason I find this interesting is that it relates to something we care about in AI: how do you robustly instill a value about something abstract into a learning system, without hand-specifying the representation? Evolution apparently solved this, with remarkably few bits, and it does so reliably. I'd love to understand how. I think it's one of those questions where an answer would be really illuminating.

r001.rationale: The response discusses brain plasticity and connectivity, but does not say that local cortical connections cluster neurons with shared functions into brain regions.

r002.rationale: It speculates that a brain region representing social information could be wired to the reward system, but does not clearly say that evolution specifies a brain location whose activity determines what is cared about.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I mean, it's a really interesting question. So let's think about it. Evolution had to solve a pretty hard problem. Social standing, how people see you, how you're regarded by others in your tribe, these are very abstract things. Where you are in the social hierarchy isn't something you can see or touch. It's a complicated computation that your brain performs, which combines lots of subtle cues. And yet evolution somehow managed to make us care about it a lot. People care about their status tremendously. And this is the mystery. How do you hardwire a desire for something that is itself an output of a very complicated neural network that evolution didn't design directly? Because the genome can't say, "here is the representation of social status, go optimize it." The representation is learned.

So I think the honest answer is, I don't know how it's done. But I think there's an intuition, which is something like this. Maybe there is some kind of mechanism where the genome gets to point at some part of the learned representation, in a fairly indirect, fairly cheap way. For example, maybe there's a region of the brain that evolves to be involved in computing things about other people, about faces, about social situations, and the genome just wires up a reward signal to that region. It doesn't need to know exactly what the computation is. It just needs to know roughly where it will end up being computed. And then the learning does the rest.

And I think this is actually relevant to AI, because it would be an existence proof. It would tell you that it's possible to specify a value function that refers to a high-level learned concept without actually having a good specification of that concept in advance. You get it kind of for free from the structure of the learning. And if evolution could do that with something as fuzzy as social standing, then maybe there's hope that we could do something similar, where the thing you care about is specified in a robust way that generalizes, rather than through some explicit formula that breaks as soon as the situation changes.

But I want to be careful. This is speculation. I don't think anyone really understands the mechanism. It's one of those things where you look at it and you say, this is clearly possible because it happened, but we don't know how, and that itself is interesting.

r001.rationale: The response does not explain that predominantly local cortical connections cluster neurons with shared functions into brain regions.

r002.rationale: It suggests the genome could wire a reward signal to a roughly specified brain region, making us care about what that region computes.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s a real mystery. It’s easy to imagine how evolution could make you care about something like hunger. There’s a signal from your body, and your brain is wired to respond to it. But consider wanting other people to think well of you. To even figure out what someone thinks of you requires a very complicated computation. So how does evolution specify that you should care about the output of that computation?

One possibility is that evolution doesn’t need to specify the computation itself. It could set up a learning process where simpler signals—approval, affection, rejection—eventually attach value to these more abstract things. But then you have to explain why that learning process reliably produces the particular motivations that it does.

I don’t think we have a complete explanation. The interesting thing is that evolution clearly can do this, somehow. And understanding how would tell us something quite fundamental about how motivations get installed in an intelligent system.

r001.rationale: The response discusses complex brain computations but does not explain that local cortical connections cluster neurons with shared functions into brain regions.

r002.rationale: It suggests learned signals may attach value to abstract outcomes, but does not propose tying caring to activity at a genetically specified brain location.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s a real mystery. Evolution can easily make you care about something like hunger, because there are fairly direct signals from your body. But how does it make you care about your reputation? Your brain has to do a lot of computation just to understand what other people think of you. How does evolution get access to the result of that computation and say, “This is something you should care about”?

One possibility is that it doesn’t need to specify the whole thing. It specifies some simpler signals, and then learning builds on those signals to produce the more complicated desire. But then you still have to explain why that learning process reliably produces the particular things evolution needs. I don’t think we have a satisfying account of how that works.

r001.rationale: The response discusses hunger, reputation, and learning, but does not mention local cortical connections or neurons clustering into brain regions.

r002.rationale: It suggests simpler signals might guide learning, but does not propose tying caring to activity at a genetically specified brain location.
